results.summary: This project is a 16-bit RISC-V CPU implemented in Verilog with a 16-bit address and data interface exposed on the chip pins. It includes an assembler and a memory image, allowing programs to be assembled and executed. The CPU reads instructions and data from an external memory via the address and data pins, with a write strobe and address latch controls, and also provides an interrupt input. The documentation refers to a README for more details, but the provided text is limited, so the exact instruction set and testing procedure are not fully described here.

This Wokwi design transmits a fixed string of ASCII characters, specifically 'tiny tapeout', over a UART serial interface. It supports uppercase ASCII characters from 0x40 to 0x5F and uses switches to control load/transmit and output enable, with a seven-segment display showing segment outputs. Testing is performed in the Wokwi simulator by setting the baud rate to 300 and toggling the switches; garbage characters may appear on initialization. The design is notable for being a simple UART transmitter that operates at a very low clock frequency of 1 Hz.

This Wokwi project is a customizable UART transmitter that can send multiple ASCII characters by storing each character in a column of flip-flops. The characters can be modified by changing the multiplexer inputs to VCC or GND, and additional characters can be added by copying and pasting columns. Testing involves setting the baud rate to 300, toggling switches for load/transmit and output enable, and observing the serial output in the Wokwi Arduino serial monitor. The documentation notes that garbage characters may be printed upon initialization, and the 'How it works' section is marked as TODO:FIXME, indicating incomplete documentation.

This Wokwi design implements a simple padlock or safe code lock that displays status on a seven-segment display. The user sets a code using switches, locks and unlocks with another switch, and enters the code with a push button. The design includes a reset switch and an LED to indicate locked status; testing involves simulating the switch and button sequences in Wokwi. It is a basic educational example of a code-based lock with minimal documentation beyond the controls description.

This Wokwi project implements a 4x4 memory using 16 flip-flops, with switches to select lines and set bits, and a read/write control. The outputs show the stored values on a seven-segment display and additional inverted bits. Testing is done by setting switches to store data and observing the display, and the design includes a truth table for operation. The documentation is adapted from an SRAM cell structure, but it is a simple educational memory test rather than a full SRAM.

This Wokwi design implements an 8-bit 4-input sorting network that orders four input numbers from highest to lowest. It uses compare-swap circuits built from full adders and multiplexers, with a carry signal selecting the multiplexer output. Testing involves applying a reset, entering four 8-bit inputs over 8 clock cycles, then enabling the load signal for 8 cycles to see the sorted outputs. The design is a compact combinatorial circuit for sorting four values, but external hardware such as switches and displays would be needed to use it interactively.

This Wokwi design is a multi-channel pulse counter with serial output, counting pulses on four input channels within a time interval measured by an RTC. It includes four 12-bit counters, overflow detection, and a state machine that periodically reads out the RTC time and counter values serially. Testing involves applying short pulses to the input channels and clocking out the serial data when overflow is signaled; the design is an early work-in-progress for a low-power sensor interface for acoustic emission detection. It is notable for its application in sensor interfaces and non-destructive testing, though the documentation notes it is a work in progress.
